extracted.intended_audience: pro se inventors / applicants drafting utility patent claims (USPTO audience)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for preparing and formatting independent and dependent claims in a non‑provisional utility patent application, including substantive claim content, structure (preamble/transition/body), and common drafting cautions. Intended to help inventors (especially pro se) craft claims that conform to USPTO requirements and practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: At least one claim required
rubrics_metrics.description: A non-provisional utility patent application must have at least one claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims define the scope of the invention and what aspects are legally protected and enforceable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim formatting and presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Start claims on a separate sheet with the heading 'claim listing' or 'claims'; each claim must begin with a capital letter and end with a period; periods may not be used elsewhere in the claims except for abbreviations; where there are several claims, they shall be numbered consecutively in Arabic numerals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where a claim sets forth a plurality of elements or steps, each element or step of the claim should be separated by a line indentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent vs dependent claim form
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims may be written in independent or dependent form. An independent claim is a stand alone claim that contains all the subject matter necessary to define the invention. A dependent claim refers to a previous claim and specifies a further limitation of the subject matter claimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dependent claims must have proper antecedent basis and should specify a further limitation; use correct dependent transitions (e.g., 'The device of claim 1, wherein...').

rubrics_metrics.name: Particularity and distinctness of claims
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim(s) shall particularly point out and distinctly claim the subject matter which the inventor regards as his invention or discovery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims must conform to the invention as set forth in the specification and the terms and phrases used in the claims must find clear support in the description so that the meaning of the terms in the claims may be ascertainable by reference to the description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims must conform to specification/support requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim or claims must conform to the invention as set forth in the specification; claim terms and phrases must find clear support in the description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure claim terms have support in the written description so that their meaning is ascertainable by reference to the specification (avoid unsupported claim terms).

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory categories for claimed subject matter
rubrics_metrics.description: The claimed invention must be to one of four categories: method/process claims, machine/apparatus, article of manufacture/device, or composition of matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Method/process claims: directed to series of acts/steps for performing desired functions. Machine/apparatus: directed to elements or components comprising the apparatus. Article of manufacture/device: directed to structure and functional components of a device or manufactured article. Composition of matter: directed to compositions/mixtures (may include chemical formulas or ingredient lists).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-claim invention review
rubrics_metrics.description: Before writing claims, answer: What is the invention? What are the pieces and parts that make up the invention? How do the pieces and parts relate to one another? Do you have more than one invention? Product: apparatus, machine, composition. Method: making or using. Are there multiple versions of each invention?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these questions to identify fundamental elements, relationships, and whether multiple inventions/versions exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preamble considerations (limiting vs non-limiting)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim usually begins with a preamble (introductory phrase). The claim preamble must be read in the context of the entire claim: terminology in the preamble that limits the structure or is intrinsically linked to the body is given patentable weight; terminology that merely recites purpose or intended use and does not add structure is not considered a limitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'A device…' (does not add structure) vs 'A device to be worn by a user…' (adds structure and limits scope).

rubrics_metrics.name: Transition phrase choice and meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim usually includes a transition phrase. Common transitions: 'comprising', 'consisting essentially of', and 'consisting of.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'Comprising' is open-ended (includes but not limited to recited elements) and is generally most commonly used. 'Consisting of' is closed-ended and excludes additional unrecited elements. 'Consisting essentially of' limits scope to specified materials/steps and those that do not materially affect the basic and novel characteristic(s); it is a middle ground. Absent clear indication in the specification of what the basic and novel characteristics are, 'consisting essentially of' may be construed as equivalent to 'comprising'. Avoid non-standard transitional phrases (may raise interpretation questions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Body of the claim: limitations and interrelationships
rubrics_metrics.description: The body follows the transitional phrase and recites the limitations (structure/elements or acts/steps) in clear, full, and concise terms necessary to define the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The body should not merely be a list of components or steps; it should recite how the essential elements are interrelated. For composition claims, include chemical formula or list of ingredients where appropriate. Where a claim sets forth a plurality of elements or steps, each element or step should end with a semicolon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependent claim drafting and transitions
rubrics_metrics.description: When adding a component in a dependent claim use 'further comprising' and explain how it is connected; when further describing something already introduced use 'wherein.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notice dependent transitions. Ensure each dependent claim has antecedent basis and includes all limitations of the claim from which it depends as a further limitation. (See 35 U.S.C. 112(d), MPEP 608.01(n)). Avoid referring back to only a portion of another claim in a dependent claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on the inventive concept
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify the features that set the invention apart from prior inventions; identify fundamental elements and omit unnecessary elements unless needed to distinguish over prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select broad terms and identify their relationships carefully; remove unnecessary claim limitations to maximize appropriate scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outline-based drafting and alignment with specification
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider drafting an outline of the invention first and then claims based on terms used in the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Think about the legal protection desired and tailor claims accordingly; look at claims in patents issued in your field of technology; review and reconcile both specification and claims, making necessary additions and corrections so claim terms find support in the specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mixing statutory classes in a single claim
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid claims covering multiple statutory classes of invention (e.g., 'A widget and method for using same…').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims should be confined to a single statutory category per claim to avoid problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid inconsistent terminology
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid the use of terms inconsistently between the claims and/or specification (e.g., visor, visor member, visor section, removable visor portion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use consistent terms throughout specification and claims to prevent ambiguity and indefiniteness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid improper dependent claim referencing
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not refer back to only a portion of another claim in a dependent claim (e.g., 'The widget of the apparatus of claim 1…').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dependent claims should properly reference the entire claim on which they depend.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'removing' or 'replacing' elements in dependent claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not 'remove' or 'replace' elements from another claim within a dependent claim (e.g., 'The vehicle of claim 1 where the removable top portion is non-removable').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dependent claims must add limitations, not contradict or improperly amend the claim they depend from.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid non-limiting/optional language that fails to limit
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use language that merely suggests or makes optional and, thus, does not limit the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure claim language actually imposes the intended limitation rather than merely suggesting it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unsupported negative limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid using negative limitations unless clearly supported by the written disclosure (specification and drawings).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Negative limitations must have clear support in the disclosure to be allowable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid purely functional language without structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use functional language that is unconnected to the structure or steps that perform the function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims should recite structure or steps corresponding to claimed functions; purely functional recitations can be problematic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unsupported terms, trademarks, and tradenames
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use terms in the claim that are unsupported by the specification; do not use trademarks or tradenames in the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use generic terms (e.g., 'hook and loop fastener' instead of Velcro.®) and ensure all claim terms have support in the specification.
